newsitem.title: UK: EMERGING MARKET OUTLOOK-Hunt for New Year bargains.
newsitem.headline: EMERGING MARKET OUTLOOK-Hunt for New Year bargains.

text.p: Emerging market investors will return to the fray this week hunting for cheap markets with solid fundamentals for some early investment plays, though a swathe of U.S. data may temper such decisions, strategists say.

How U.S. markets perform this week, after strong housing sales data wiped over a point off U.S. Treasuries in an unpleasant New Year's Eve surprise, will help determine which will be the markets of choice for the start of 1997.

U.S. figures due this week include factory goods orders on Tuesday, producer prices on Thursday and payroll numbers on Friday. All will be closely watched for clues to the U.S. Federal Reserve's next move amid speculation it may soon raise official interest rates.
But this is unlikely to deflect eager investors from New Year bargain-hunting, with plenty of time to recoup losses from any injudicious selections.
"You often get a rally in the early part of January with people getting aggressive on their investment decisions," said Nigel Rendell, emerging market strategist at HSBC James Capel.
"People will be looking for those markets that look cheap but have good fundamentals."

He pointed to POLAND and HUNGARY in particular as ready to hear some good news from foreign portfolio managers. "They both have good fundamentals and single figure price/earnings ratios in 1997," Rendell said.

They, and even countries like ROMANIA with a new right-wing government in place, will look more appealing to investors than BULGARIA, which is still struggling with a protracted economic crisis complicated by the resignation of Prime Minister Zhan Videnov more than two weeks ago.
Bulgaria's ruling Socialists are expected to propose a new premier on Friday.

Last week's collapse of the lev to a record 600 to the dollar is showing debt market investors how hard Sofia will find it to meet its January 28 Brady bond interest payments in the absence of a crucial loan from the International Monetary Fund.
"Given the political upheavals in the country, it is doubtful whether the IMF will make a further disbursement in time to meet this payment," WestMerchant Capital Markets said.
In Latin America, ARGENTINA rather than BRAZIL looks like the investment market of choice, analysts said.

"Brazil is a high risk bet for a short term investment -- they will be concentrating on reform, which has been going fairly slowly, and on (President Fernando Henrique Cardoso's) mandate for reelection," said Rendell.
"People are more optimistic on Argentina with its economic pick-up gathering momentum."
Argentina is rumoured to be readying a $2 billion global bond, with a five and 20-year tranche, for launch possibly as early as this week.
Also imminent is a jumbo $1.0 billion global bond which MEXICO plans to launch on Wednesday, likely to provide an early filip to the country's Brady debt market.
Looking further ahead, however, WestMerchant Capital Markets warned that politics in Mexico could destabilise the emerging country debt market this year.

"There can be little doubt that, as regards country fundamentals, one of the major threats to the emerging country debt market in 1997 will be the political turbulence in Mexico," WestMerchant said in a note to investors.
Mid-term congressional elections loom in July, and the country is also due to hold its first election for governor of Mexico City.
"Facing the prospect of defeat, the ruling PRI party is unlikely to relinquish power graciously," WestMerchant said. But it added this was unlikely to derail economic recovery.
PERU is likely to feel the effect in investment terms this month of its protracted hostage crisis, which dragged on, unresolved, into 1997 after its outbreak on December 17.
"Everybody thought that Peru had made giant steps forward, shaking off the terrorism that had plagued the country for years," one Latin American strategist said.
"When something like this happens it sets the country back quite a way, and I think that's going to frighten a lot of people off."
But investors are bullish on RUSSIA, which put in a stunning performance on JP Morgan's emerging debt index to show gains of 113.4 percent over 1996.
With President Boris Yeltsin now back at work and prospects in sight for an end to recession, selected stocks are likely to be in strong demand as the year opens.
HSBC James Capel is looking for the first year of positive growth in Russia after seven years in negative territory, forecasting 3.0 percent growth for 1997.
Analysts said service industry stocks rather than the traditional industries were likely to benefit most.

TURKEY may prove another short-term winner. Rendell recommended its markets as a trading buy rather than an aggressive long-term hold, adding prices were relatively cheap and the economic situation appeared less grave than hitherto believed.
The IFC emerging market composite investable index, IFC/IPRD, denominated in dollars, was up 1.4 percent week-on-week at 295.80 points after Friday's close.
Latin America was up 1.7 percent week-on-week at 541.59, Asia was up 1.4 percent at 252.80 and Europe, Middle East and Africa as a region was up 1.2 at 134.56.
